compressed_text: Volkswagen announced on September 26, 2025, it will pause production for one week in early October at its Zwickau and Dresden electric car plants in Germany, citing adaptation to market conditions. Bloomberg reported a similar shutdown at VW's Emden plant, though VW declined to confirm. The move reflects weak European EV demand due to high costs and sparse charging infrastructure. It follows Bosch's announcement of 10% German job cuts and Ford's plan to cut up to 1,000 jobs at its Cologne EV plant, partly due to weak EV demand. VW had previously agreed to cut 35,000 jobs by 2030 and faces competition in China and weak European demand.

Japan production dropped to 44,586 units (88.4% YoY), its first YoY decline in three months; year-to-date Japan output was 438,531 units (98.5% of 2024). Production outside Japan totaled 222,419 units (86.7% YoY, 13th straight month down). Regional output: North America 136,559 units (94.9% YoY, US 88,056 units at 93.9% YoY); Asia 76,887 units (74.3% YoY, China 50,011 units at 80.5% YoY). Contrastingly, exports from Japan surged to 7,307 units (126.9% YoY), the fifth consecutive increase. North America received 2,037 units (+270.2% YoY, US 1,727 units +236.6%). Japan domestic sales fell 8% to 301,221 units.

compressed_text: European carmakers face potential manufacturing disruption due to a dispute over chipmaker Nexperia, the EU auto association ACEA warned on Oct. 17. The Dutch government took control of Chinese-owned Nexperia on Sept. 30, citing technology transfer risks to parent Wingtech, which the U.S. placed on its entity list in December. In response, China on Oct. 4 banned Nexperia China from exporting certain components. Last week, Nexperia notified carmakers it could no longer guarantee chip delivery. Without these chips, European suppliers cannot build parts, threatening production stoppages. ACEA urged immediate resolution to avoid further strain on an industry already battling tariffs, foreign competition, and weak demand.

compressed_text: Ford reduced its Dearborn F-150 Lightning plant workforce to one-third of 2,100 employees, transferring or offering early retirement to the rest. This follows a September 16 fire at Novelis' Oswego mill, which supplies 40% of U.S. automotive aluminum and will remain inoperable until early 2026. The disruption forces Ford to prioritize gasoline F-series trucks and idle EV production. Demand for the F-150 Lightning has crashed, leading to slashed production targets. The aluminum crisis could cost Ford $500 million to $1 billion in lost earnings and threatens Super Duty production. Ford's stock dropped 10% since the fire. Broader supply-chain vulnerabilities, including semiconductor shortages, compound the crisis.

The decision leaves ~600 workers’ future uncertain and blindsided Unifor Local 88, which called it devastating. GM is not moving production elsewhere and will assess the plant’s future. compressed_text: Volkswagen Group plans to invest 160 billion euros ($186 billion) through 2030, CEO Oliver Blume announced, reflecting belt-tightening as Europe's top automaker faces a major crisis in China and the United States. The total is down from 180 billion euros for 2024-2028, which marked a peak. Volkswagen has been squeezed by US tariffs and fierce competition in China, hurting profits especially at Porsche, which sells around half its cars in these markets and unveiled a major roll-back on its EV strategy. He added that localising production in the wider Volkswagen group and a tailor-made Porsche model for China could make sense.

The deal collapsed after Indian authorities seized manufacturing assets on national-security grounds; Luxshare sought arbitration in Singapore in January 2026 to reclaim its deposit, with Wingtech counterclaiming.
